title: Lockstep to Async Scaling: exploration and field notes
body:
Purpose
---
Quick field notes from a set of runs comparing lockstep (synchronous tensor/pipeline sync points) vs more asynchronous scheduling strategies for multi-GPU LLM inference. Focus is on tail-latency behavior with small interleaved batches and the interplay with interconnect arbitration (NVSwitch/NVLink rings, PCIe host transfer), NCCL collective scheduling jitter, and KV-cache coherence gating.

Why this felt necessary
- Several customer incidents where p50 looked fine but p99/p999 spiked unpredictably during mixed short/long sequences.
- Existing NCCL-centric writeups explain some microbursts but not the long-tailed stalls we see when we try to break lockstep across pipeline partitions.
- We need actionable knobs that operations or runtime can flip: prefer async overlap, or enforce strict barrier alignment.

Hypothesis
- Strict lockstep across GPUs tends to concentrate synchronization points; when interconnect contention or host DMA delays occur those barriers amplify stalls across all replicas (all GPUs wait).
- Allowing controlled asynchrony (staggered KV-cache install, pipelined micro-batches) will reduce global stalls but increases variance per-request; there is a sweet spot where average cost reduces and tails stay acceptable.

Environment & test harness
- Hardware: 8x A100-80GB within a single NVSwitch pod, PCIe root complexes connected to two hosts (host-side staging for batching).
- OS/driver: Ubuntu 22.04, NVIDIA driver 535.x, CUDA 12.1, NCCL 2.18.
- Runtime: local branch with scheduling hooks (github PR referenced above) that can toggle: strict_barrier=true/false, kv_install_mode={blocking, async_prefetch, staged}, pipeline_stagger_ms=[0,1,2,4,8].
- Load generator: synthetic LLM workload reproducing a stop/start pattern: 60% short prompts (16 tokens), 30% medium (128 tokens), 10% long (1024 tokens). QPS held ~120. We sweep batch sizes and interleaving.

Measurements collected
- Per-GPU occupancy and compute utilization (nvidia-smi sampled at 100ms), NvSwitch counters (aggregate bisection utilization), PCIe DMA stalls (from perf and driver logs), and NCCL trace timelines (nsys).
- Inference-level metrics: per-request latency distribution, model-token throughput, kv-cache hit/miss counts, and a simple quality signal (probability calibration drift - synthetic).

Representative run notes (short summary)
1) Baseline (strict_barrier=true, kv_install=blocking, pipeline_stagger=0)
- p50: 48ms, p95: 93ms, p99: 220ms, p999: 870ms.
- Observations: periodic 700-900ms stalls correlated with host PCIe queuing spikes; NVSwitch bisection under 65% normally but shows short spikes aligned to NCCL AllGather boundaries.
- nvprof/nsys timeline: all GPUs idle waiting on an AllGather completion for 350-900us in some windows — these stack across many requests due to lockstep.

2) Staggered pipeline (strict_barrier=true, pipeline_stagger=4ms)
- p50: 51ms, p95: 78ms, p99: 160ms, p999: 420ms.
- Notes: tail significantly improved. The stagger reduces simultaneous NVSwitch storms and host DMA bursts. However, we observed slight increased jitter for short-prompts when they coincided with stagger boundaries.

3) Asynchronous KV install (strict_barrier=false, kv_install_mode=async_prefetch, pipeline_stagger=2ms)
- p50: 46ms, p95: 70ms, p99: 130ms, p999: 280ms.
- Notes: further reduction in tails; NCCL activity is smeared out which helps interconnect arbitration. But occasional KV coherence re-fetches (observed as extra PCIe reads) caused ~150-300ms anomalies when async prefetch raced with a model switch.

4) Aggressive async (strict_barrier=false, kv_install_mode=staged, pipeline_stagger=0)
- p50: 44ms, p95: 76ms, p99: 210ms, p999: 640ms.
- Notes: average improved but long tail returned in a different mode: instead of joint barrier stalls, we saw per-GPU long stalls when a prefetch failed and blocked at the compute boundary. This implies extra complexity from local error handling.

Key qualitative observations
- Lockstep creates correlated waiting: once one GPU hits a host DMA queue delay, the effect fans out. This is visible as high cross-correlation in the NCCL trace (every timeline shows a simultaneous gap).
- Staggering by a few ms reduces simultaneous pressure on NVSwitch and host I/O enough to cut tails in half in many runs. The optimal stagger depends on batch size and sequence length mix; typical sweet spot: 2-6ms for our workload.
- Async KV install reduces synchronized AllGather timings and smooths traffic, but requires more robust coherence/failure handling to avoid per-device long stalls.
- NCCL scheduling jitter is amplified by driver-level DMA scheduling. We observed that enabling some host-side submission aggregation (coalescing small host-to-device transfers) also reduced tails.

Practical knobs and tradeoffs (operational summary)
- If the product priority is minimizing worst-case p999 for mixed short/long workloads: prefer mild staggering + blocking KV install (stagger 3-5ms). This avoids decentralized prefetch failures while breaking exact lockstep.
- If average cost matters more than absolute tails: enable async prefetch with backstop timeouts + retry logic, allow more asynchrony to increase throughput and lower p50/p95.
- For predictable throughput at large reserved capacity: pair scheduling tweaks with host transfer batching (coalesce small DMA) and careful NCCL tuning (turn down high-frequency collective retries).

Open questions / TODOs
- Need a formal microbenchmark to isolate host DMA queuing: synthetic host-only DMA flood to measure queuing delays under various kernel submission patterns.
- Check NVSwitch QoS settings (if any operated by cloud provider) and reproduce across two different physical pod topologies (flattened ring vs multi-island).
- Measure energy/cost delta for async prefetch strategy — does extra DMA traffic materially increase unit cost? Add token-cost calculations.
- Consider runtime invariant: enforce a maximal per-request stagger variance (e.g., jitter cap) to avoid pathological request slowdown when many small prompts align.

Immediate action items
- Miguel: create microbenchmark harness for host DMA queueing by 2025-08-15 (JIRA-RT-1983).
- Aisha: instrument KV-install to emit per-step telemetry (prefetch start, complete, retry) and add counters to console dashboards by 2025-08-18.
- Priya: run a 24-hour soak with async_prefetch + staged backoff on a customer-candidate stack and collect p99/p999 across varying qps (JIRA-RT-1985).

Notes to self
- Save NCCL traces with absolute timestamps; relative traces hide cross-host DMA alignment.
- When re-running, toggle nsys sampling at 10ms resolution for timeline clarity.
- Remember to record which firmware revision on host NICs — DMA scheduling differences are subtle and may depend on NIC driver.

Appendix: quick commands used
- nsys profile --trace=cuda,nccl -o out --sample=cpu --stats=true --duration=60s
- simple host DMA flood (low-level): small loop writing pinned buffers via cudaMemcpyAsync + cudaStreamSynchronize to emulate many small host submissions.

End of notes. This doc is intentionally informal; will extract a runbook after the soak and when we have deterministic microbenchmark outputs.
